title: ARTEX gets an FBI detection pack and a cloud foothold
overview: The FBI's ARTEX advisory brings fresh detection work, while Barracuda discloses an intrusion through an unrevoked supplier key. Four DrayTek fixes, a TSMC employee data leak and an Apache Shiro authentication bypass round out the morning.
paragraphs: Good morning, it's 5:22 AM. Monday, the sixteenth of November, twenty twenty-six.

That ARTEX exposed-console story from last Sunday now comes with something you can put to work: a thirteen-page FBI FLASH advisory, released on Friday, and an open-source detection pack from MalwareMustDie. The console count has climbed to more than sixteen hundred. The bureau dates weaponisation of the AI penetration-testing framework to at least August, and names Huntress's finding of at least a hundred and sixty-two compromised ConnectWise tenants.

The useful change isn't just another warning about automated attacks. You've now got command-and-control indicators and suspicious network activity to hunt for, alongside a playbook that grades indicators by confidence. The FBI warns that infrastructure addresses may already have aged. I'd load the pack, but I wouldn't treat a clean search for those IPs as a clean bill of health. Give the behavioural rules some attention: bursts of automated requests and unexpected privilege changes are worth investigating even when the address isn't on yesterday's list. The pack also covers identity abuse and cloud activity. If you run internet-facing applications or cloud administration interfaces, use it to focus a review of application permissions and authentication logs; report findings to the FBI or IC3. That's a rather more useful Monday job than counting exposed consoles.

And ARTEX has turned up inside a security vendor's own cloud. Barracuda says an intruder reached ten cloud environments, some managing its XDR platform, during almost two days of access this month. The way in? A cloud key issued to an AI service provider that Barracuda forgot to revoke when the work ended. The provider alerted it on the fourth of November; Barracuda hasn't named that provider. Once inside, the attacker deployed ARTEX and went hunting for crypto seed phrases and private keys.

The worrying reach is through XDR integration credentials into customer environments. Barracuda says it found no evidence those credentials were accessed, although some customers were told to reissue them anyway. If you got that notification, do it today. And I'd check supplier keys whose contracts have ended: the paperwork can say goodbye while the key still says hello.

That closes a cloud door; on the network edge, there's a single firmware update worth moving along. DrayTek's Vigor2960 small-office router has four critical flaws, each scoring nine point nine, with public exploits for all four. They sit in the same mainfunction CGI script and can be reached remotely with low privileges. One upload argument permits command injection, meaning commands can run on the router itself. Two other flaws allow path traversal; a file-existence check also has a heap overflow through its upload_name argument. Public exploits aren't confirmation of attacks in the wild, but they're plenty of reason not to leave this waiting. If you run firmware 1 point 5 point 1 point 0 through 1 point 5 point 1 point 6, upgrade to 1 point 5 point 1 point 7. One build fixes the lot. Keep that web console off the public internet as well.

Back on the supplier side, TSMC has confirmed a leak of current and former employees' personal data after six point nine gigabytes were offered at auction, saying it matches data held by a cloud service provider. There's nothing to patch here; warn affected staff about identity and payroll fraud.

There is a patch for an equally uncomfortable identity problem in Apache Shiro, the Java security framework: with LDAP authentication caching explicitly enabled, one successful login lets later attempts for that username succeed with any password because the cache skips the LDAP bind. CVE-2026-129349 scores nine point one; if you use DefaultLdapRealm or JndiLdapRealm with that non-default setting, upgrade from 3 point 0 point 0 or earlier to 3 point 0 point 1, or disable authentication caching on the realm.

I'd get the exposed DrayTek consoles out of reach while the firmware change goes through. For the ARTEX hunt, keep the confidence ratings beside the matches; an old address needs context, not an automatic verdict. Hope your Monday starts quietly.
